opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's honestly one of the trickiest parts of working on post-training at a frontier lab, because you're never really training in isolation. When I'm working on something like a new behavior or a product feature, say making the model better at a particular kind of writing or a canvas-style interaction, I'm adding data to a mixture that a lot of other people are also contributing to. And the capabilities they care about, like coding or math or refusals, aren't things I deeply own or have intuition for.

So the first thing is that you lean really heavily on shared evals. Most teams maintain their own eval suites for the capabilities they own, and the culture is that before you ship a change to the data mix, you run the broad set of evals and look at the deltas. If coding drops a couple of points or refusal rates shift, that's a signal you need to go investigate, even if it's not your area.

The second thing is that you actually talk to people. If I see a regression in something I don't understand well, the fastest path is usually to ping the person who owns that capability and ask, "Hey, does this look like noise to you, or is this real?" They have context on variance, on which evals are flaky, on what a meaningful drop looks like. I think a lot of model development is honestly a social process in that way.

And then the third piece is building your own lightweight checks for the interactions you're worried about. Like if I'm teaching the model to be more proactive or ask more clarifying questions, I might worry that it'll start asking clarifying questions in a coding context where that's really annoying. So I'll write a small set of targeted prompts that probe the boundary between my behavior and someone else's domain. That's often where regressions show up: not in the core capability, but in the seams where behaviors conflict.

I'd also say you have to be kind of humble about it. Quantitative evals don't catch everything, so I spend a lot of time just reading model outputs, doing vibes checks across different kinds of prompts. Sometimes you notice the model got a little more verbose or a little weirder in tone before any benchmark picks it up. That qualitative sense matters a lot, especially for things like personality and writing, where the metrics are still pretty immature.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared evals, consulting capability owners, targeted prompts, and qualitative output reviews. It does not identify dataset ablation as an approach.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is actually one of the hardest parts of the job, and I think it's underappreciated how much of post-training is really about this coordination problem rather than any single clever technique.

The way I think about it is that when you're pushing on one capability, say you own something like instruction-following or a particular behavior, you're almost never changing just that thing. You're changing the data mixture, you're changing the reward signal, and all of that has downstream effects on things you didn't intend to touch. Coding might get slightly worse, or the model becomes more verbose, or it starts refusing things it shouldn't. And the tricky part is that the people who actually understand those other capabilities deeply, who know what "good" looks like for them, are different people, often on different teams.

So the first thing is you have to accept that you can't be an expert in everything, and you have to build a very explicit notion of what the key evals are across the whole organization. Not a hundred evals, because then nobody looks at them, but a small set that each team basically signs off on as "this is the thing that, if it drops, we care." And you treat those as a gate. Before anything gets merged into the main mixture, you run that suite and you look at it honestly, not just at the metric you were optimizing for.

The second thing, and I think this matters a lot, is that the metrics alone are usually not enough. Automated evals have blind spots, they saturate, they get gamed accidentally. So I spend a huge amount of time just reading transcripts. Side-by-side outputs from the old model and the new one, on prompts that aren't from my own domain. You develop an intuition pretty fast for when something feels off, even if you can't yet articulate what the regression is. And then you go to the team that owns that area and say, hey, I'm seeing this, does this match what you'd expect? That conversation is often more informative than any dashboard.

And the third piece is culturally you have to make it low-cost for people to flag regressions to you and vice versa. If I'm scared of breaking someone else's thing, I'll be too conservative. If they're scared of telling me I broke it, it ships. So you want the norm to be: everybody is sort of jointly responsible for the model as a whole, and the data ownership is more about who's accountable for improving it than who's allowed to notice when it's wrong.

r001.rationale: The response describes organization-wide evals, transcript reviews, and cross-team coordination, but does not identify dataset ablation as an approach.

astra-6.text:
I think the first step is working with the people who own those capabilities, because you’re not going to have all the data or all the context yourself. You need to understand what they consider a regression and which evaluations actually capture that.

Then, when you make a change, you want to look beyond the capability you’re trying to improve. If your target metric goes up, what happens elsewhere? And if something drops, I’d look at concrete examples with the relevant team to understand whether it’s a meaningful loss or noise in the evaluation. It’s really a shared process of making those tradeoffs visible.

r001.rationale: The response describes collaborating with capability owners, reviewing evaluations, and inspecting examples, but it does not identify dataset ablation as an approach.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the hard part is that you don’t necessarily know what you’re breaking. You might be improving the capability you’re focused on, but somebody else has a set of use cases that you don’t have visibility into. So you need to work closely with the people who own those areas and have them evaluate the model on their data. You can’t just look at your own evaluations and conclude that the model is better overall.

And when a regression shows up, you need to look at the actual examples. Is this a real capability regression, or is the model responding differently in a way that the evaluation doesn’t capture well? That distinction matters before you decide what to change.

r001.rationale: The response recommends having capability owners evaluate the model on their data and inspecting regression examples, but it does not identify dataset ablation as an approach.
